1.title: Value Co-Creation and Service Relationships
1.text: Welcome to Module two: Value Co-Creation and Service Relationships. It covers the exam area Key eye til terms and definitions. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. Define value, value co-creation, cost, risk, output and outcome. Explain how outcomes, costs, risks, utility, warranty, user experience, sustainability and feedback contribute to value co-creation. Define organization, service provider, service consumer, digital product vendor, the three relationship types, the service journey, sponsor, customer, user, service quality, service level and S L A (service level agreement). Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Key eye til terms and definitions (thirty percent). Exam format: forty multiple-choice questions in sixty minutes; twenty-six correct answers (sixty-five percent) pass. Validated against: the official eye til Foundation (Version five) syllabus, version five point zero (February two thousand twenty-six).

1.title: Value and co-creation
1.text: Value and co-creation. Value is the perceived benefit, usefulness and importance of something. Value co-creation means value is created together by the provider and the consumer, through activities and interactions, not handed over by the provider alone. Output. A tangible or intangible deliverable of an activity (a report, a working feature). Outcome. A result for a stakeholder enabled by one or more outputs (faster orders, fewer errors). Cost. What the consumer spends or gives up (money, time, effort), including the cost of creating the value. Risk. A possible event that could cause harm or make achieving objectives harder. Exam tip: Output equals what you get. Outcome equals what changes because of it. A new report is an output; better decisions are the outcome.

1.title: What contributes to value
1.text: What contributes to value. The figure shows this: Value co-creation: outcomes, costs, risks, utility, warranty, experience, sustainability and feedback.

1.title: What contributes to value, continued
1.text: What contributes to value. Outcomes. The results the consumer wants. Costs. Lower or justified costs raise perceived value. Risks. Lower risk raises value. Utility. The product does what is needed. Warranty. It is available and dependable. User experience. It is pleasant and easy to use. Sustainability. It can be sustained over time without harm. Feedback. Information from consumers shapes improvement and keeps the work aimed at value.

1.title: Who is who
1.text: Who is who. Organization. A person or group with its own functions, responsibilities and goals. Service provider. An organization that provides services to consumers. Service consumer. An organization or person that consumes services. Digital product vendor. An organization that supplies digital products (often as goods or access to resources). A service provider runs the service for you. A digital product vendor supplies the product itself. A service consumer uses either, and may be the same organization as the provider in an internal setting.

1.title: Roles of the consumer
1.text: Roles of the consumer. Sponsor. Authorizes the budget for consumption. Customer. Defines requirements and takes responsibility for the outcomes of consumption. User. Uses the services. One person can hold more than one role. Exam tip: Sponsor pays. Customer decides what is needed. User uses.

1.title: Relationship types and the service journey
1.text: Relationship types and the service journey. Basic. Transactional: the provider supplies, the consumer pays, little more. Cooperative. Mutually beneficial; the parties share information and adjust to each other. Collaborative. A partnership with shared goals and joint risk and reward. The service journey is the path a consumer and provider follow together, from the first contact to realized value. The eye til four journey steps were explore, engage, offer, agree, onboard, co-create and realize.

1.title: Service quality, service level and SLA
1.text: Service quality, service level and S L A. Service quality. How well the service meets the consumer's needs and expectations. Service level. A measurable statement of the level of service to be delivered. Service Level Agreement. A documented agreement between a provider and a customer naming the services and the expected service levels. Exam tip: An S L A is an agreement; a service level is the target inside it.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A new dashboard is delivered to the finance team, and decisions are now made two days faster. Which statement is right? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: The dashboard is the output and the faster decisions are the outcome. An output is the deliverable; the outcome is the result it enables.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Who defines the requirements for a service and takes responsibility for the outcomes of consumption? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: The customer. The customer defines requirements and takes responsibility for outcomes.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. Which statement about relationships is C O R R E C T? (one) A basic relationship is transactional. (two) A collaborative relationship is a partnership with shared goals. (three) A cooperative relationship has no sharing of information. (four) A basic relationship needs shared goals and joint risk. The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: one and two. Basic is transactional and collaborative is a partnership.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Identify the missing word(s). A blank authorizes the budget for service consumption. The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Sponsor. The sponsor authorizes the budget.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. Customers give feedback and the provider changes the product. Which idea does this show? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Value co-creation, because feedback shapes what is created. Feedback is part of how value is co-created.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. Which document names the services and the expected service levels between a provider and a customer? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: A service level agreement. That is the S L A.

1.title: Recall Check 1
1.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. Define value co-creation. Answer: Value created together by the provider and the consumer through activities and interactions. Question two. Output or outcome: a result for a stakeholder? Answer: Outcome. Question three. What does the sponsor do? Answer: Authorizes the budget for consumption.

1.title: Recall Check 2
1.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Name the three relationship types. Answer: Basic, cooperative and collaborative. Question five. What is an S L A? Answer: A documented agreement between a provider and a customer on services and expected service levels. Question six. What are the seven contributors to value? Answer: Outcomes, costs, risks, utility, warranty, user experience and sustainability (with feedback shaping them).

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Output or outcome: deliverable or result for a stakeholder. Cost or risk: what is spent or given up or possible harm. Roles: sponsor pays, customer defines needs, user uses. Relationships: basic (transaction), cooperative (mutual), collaborative (partnership). S L A: agreement; service level is the target.
